title: MEV-Boost Explained: Block Auction Towers 🗼
ig_caption:
Wait—who bids for your Ethereum block? 👀
MEV-Boost turns block building into a 12s auction.

- MEMPOOL: pending transactions swirl in the public pool
- BUILDER: builds the most profitable block (captures MEV)
- SEALED BID + SIGNED HEADER: builder sends a bid without revealing everything publicly
- RELAY: routes the best bid to the right validator path
- PROPOSER (validator): picks the highest-value bid to propose
- PROPOSER EARNS: proposer gets paid for including the winning bid

Practical takeaway: The separation reduces transparency between builders and validators, changing MEV incentives—so measure MEV risk when designing relays, builders, and MEV-sensitive strategies.

What matters more for Ethereum: maximizing proposer revenue or minimizing MEV centralization—where should the line be?
fb_caption:
Ethereum’s MEV-Boost + proposer-builder separation is essentially “block space as a competitive auction,” repeated roughly every 12 seconds.

What’s happening (matching the reel):
- MEMPOOL: users broadcast transactions publicly, but the path to inclusion is not guaranteed.
- Builders craft candidate blocks optimized for extractable value (MEV), not just gas fees.
- Instead of validators directly choosing from mempool, builders produce a sealed set of value: a signed, sealed header + a bid.
- Relays aggregate and route these bids, selecting the most attractive option for the proposer.
- The proposer (validator) then submits the block that won the auction for that slot and earns the associated rewards.

Protocol trade-offs (why separation exists):
- Efficiency: Validators can avoid running full block construction logic and can focus on proposing/attesting.
- Incentive alignment: MEV extracted by builders is competitively bid—so rational builders pay validators via relayed value.
- Complexity & centralization pressures: bidding power can concentrate among dominant relays/builders, which may influence censorship resistance and distribution of MEV capture.
- Security boundaries: the separation changes the trust model—validators rely on the relay/builder pipeline for “who wins” the proposal, while still enforcing consensus rules on the block contents.

Tokenomics / economic implications (high level):
- No direct token “pays” here; instead, value is transferred through auction outcomes and block economics (execution tips/value → builder bids → proposer rewards). This affects how MEV revenue is distributed across actors in the ecosystem.
- Competitive auctions can increase overall proposer earnings while letting builders specialize, but can also create gatekeepers if infrastructure access becomes uneven.

Security implications to watch:
- Censorship risk: if relays/builders systematically exclude certain transactions, inclusion guarantees degrade (even if consensus is correct).
- Incentive shocks: changes to bidding logic, relay policies, or builder competition can alter which transactions get included and when.
- Attack surface shifts: rather than attacking consensus directly, adversaries target the auction pipeline (relay selection, bid propagation, and builder dominance).

Key takeaway: MEV-Boost improves how value is discovered and distributed for block proposals, but it also reshapes Ethereum’s trust assumptions—so any DeFi strategy that relies on ordering, inclusion timing, or fair execution should account for MEV-auction dynamics.

Debate: Should Ethereum optimize for maximum proposer revenue (auction power) or stronger decentralization/neutrality (constraining relay/builder influence)?
threads_caption: MEV-Boost = Ethereum auctions block space every ~12s. Builders send sealed bids, relays route winners, validators (proposers) pick the top value. More revenue—or more centralization? Where do you stand?
